The Keeper's Ledgers

The ferry to Carrow Island ran twice a day in summer and, after the first week of October, only when the harbormaster felt like it. Nora Pell took the 7:40 crossing on a Tuesday, with one suitcase, a borrowed raincoat and a letter from a solicitor she had never met.

The letter was short. Her great-uncle, Edmund Pell, had died in March at the age of 91. He had left her the keeper's cottage at Carrow Light, its contents, and "such papers as may be found therein." There was no money to speak of. There was, the solicitor added, a small matter of unpaid harbor dues amounting to £38.

She had met Edmund exactly once, at a wedding in 1987, when she was nine. He had given her a brass button and told her it came from the coat of a drowned captain. Her mother said afterwards that he had bought a bag of them in a market in Hull.

"What books?"

"The light's books. Every ship, every night." He looked out at the water. "Nobody asked him to. The light's been automatic since 1994."

The cottage stood about two hundred yards from the tower, behind a wall that had been repaired so many times it was mostly mortar. The key was under a flowerpot, which the solicitor's letter had described, with evident disapproval, as "the customary arrangement."

Inside, it smelled of paraffin and old paper. There were two rooms downstairs and one above. Every wall that did not hold a window held a shelf, and every shelf held ledgers: tall, narrow, bound in green cloth, their spines numbered in white ink. She counted 112 of them before she gave up.

She took down the nearest one. The first page was dated 3 January 1961. Below the date, in a small upright hand, her great-uncle had written the time, the wind, the state of the sea, and then a list of every vessel that had passed the light between dusk and dawn. There were eleven that night. He had noted the name of each one where he could read it, and where he could not he had written "unknown, two masts" or "unknown, coaster, heading north."

The next page was 4 January, and the page after that was the 5th. She turned to the middle of the book and then to the end. He had not missed a night.

Editor's note: the 1961 ledger is now held by the county archive, where it may be consulted by appointment.

It was the same in the next volume, and the one after. She pulled out a ledger from the far end of the highest shelf and found it only half full. The last entry was dated 9 March of the present year, eleven days before he died. Wind south-west, force 5. Sea moderate. Four vessels. The handwriting had grown larger and less steady, but the columns were as straight as ever.

Nora sat down on the bottom stair. She had come intending to stay two nights, sign whatever needed signing, and put the place up for sale. She had a job to go back to, a flat with a leaking tap, and a train booked for Thursday at 2:15 p.m.

It was the harbormaster who explained it, the following morning, over tea that was nearly black. His name was Tom Garrity and he had known Edmund for forty years. "People think he was lonely out here," he said. "He wasn't. He just liked things written down. He said if nobody wrote it down, it was as if the night hadn't happened."

"But who was it for?"

Garrity considered this. "There was a trawler went missing in 1973," he said. "The Marguerite, out of Peterhead. Six men aboard. The inquiry wanted to know if she'd passed the light, and when. Edmund had it: twenty past one in the morning, heading east, lights showing. It didn't save anybody. But the families knew how far she got." He put down his cup. "After that I stopped asking who it was for."

She did not catch the Thursday train. She told herself it was because of the weather, which was true as far as it went: the wind had gone round to the north and the ferry was not running. She spent the day carrying ledgers down to the kitchen table, twelve at a time, and reading them in order.

Most nights were dull. A few were not. In February 1968 he had counted 43 vessels sheltering in the lee of the island during a storm that lasted three days. In August 1979 he had written, without comment, "Lights seen to the west at 02:10, low on the water, not a ship." In the winter of 1985 there was a gap of a single night, and beside it, in the margin, the words "Influenza. Mrs. Garrity kept the count."

On Saturday the ferry ran again. Nora walked down to the harbor, stood for some time looking at the timetable, and then walked back up the hill. That evening, a little before dusk, she found a pencil, opened the half-filled ledger to the first empty page, and wrote the date at the top.

She did not know the proper way to describe the wind. She wrote "cold, from the right." Then she pulled a chair to the window, and waited for the first ship.
